subheads.title: 2.1 Geographic Identity and the Land Reality
paragraphs: The coordinates supplied for this assessment, 6.8868°N and 79.9187°E, reverse-geocode to Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte, Sri Lanka's administrative capital, within the Colombo District of Western Province. More precisely, the point falls along the Parliament Approach corridor, in the Pita Kotte East and Battaramulla locality, immediately beside the Diyawanna Oya wetland and the national Parliament complex. This is, in short, the institutional heart of the country — a dense urban fabric of government buildings, arterial roads, residential neighbourhoods and a legally significant body of open water. It is among the least likely locations on the island at which one would expect to assemble a contiguous parcel of land for utility-scale generation.

We must therefore open this section with a frank and unambiguous siting caveat, because it is fundamental rather than incidental. A 10 MW (ac) fixed-tilt solar plant of approximately 12 MWp DC requires a substantial, broadly contiguous, unshaded footprint — typically a tract on the order of tens of hectares once inter-row spacing, access, setbacks and balance-of-plant are accounted for. At this specific location there is realistically no such land available. The setting is a dense urban and protected-wetland environment: the Diyawanna Oya and its margins are environmentally designated open water and marsh, the surrounding land is intensively built up, and the parcels that exist are fragmented, encumbered and of high alternative value. There is, plainly, no 10 MW of developable ground here.

We make this point at the outset so that it frames everything that follows. The remainder of this report assesses the resource, technology and financial viability of a 10 MW solar plant as briefed — that is, treating the supplied coordinates as the nominated assessment location — while flagging that the land constraint is, on its own, a project-defining obstacle. A lender or developer reading this should understand that even were the economics attractive (and, as later sections show, they are not), the physical premise of siting a utility-scale array at this exact point does not survive first contact with the ground reality. Where relevant, we note that relocation is the single most powerful lever available, and we return to it in the recommendations.

subheads.title: 2.2 Climatic Zone and Resource Context
paragraphs: Beyond the question of land, the location carries a second, quieter disadvantage that is just as material to a solar assessment: its climatic zone. Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte sits within Sri Lanka's south-west wet zone, the cloudiest and rainiest region of the island and, in consequence, among its lowest-irradiance. This is not a marginal distinction. The wet zone's persistent cloud cover, high humidity and pronounced monsoonal rainfall depress the usable solar resource relative to the drier parts of the country. For a technology whose entire revenue stream is a direct function of incident irradiance, being located in the island's least-sunny quartile is a structural headwind rather than a detail of microclimate.

The contrast with Sri Lanka's better solar geographies is stark and worth stating explicitly for context. The island's strongest resource lies in the dry north-east and south-east — Vavuniya, Pooneryn and Hambantota among them — where lower cloud cover and reduced rainfall translate into materially higher annual yields. The national GHI range, per World Bank and Solargis data, spans roughly 1,247 to 2,106 kWh/m²/yr; this site, in the wet zone, sits well below the upper end of that envelope. The verified Global Solar Atlas (Solargis v2.2.68) figure for the location is an annual GHI of 1,909 kWh/m²/yr, with DNI of 1,273 and diffuse of 940 kWh/m²/yr, an average ambient temperature of 26.5°C, and an optimum tilt of around 9°. The relatively high diffuse fraction is itself a fingerprint of the cloudy, humid wet-zone climate.

What this means for the assessment is a yield that is respectable in absolute terms but unambiguously sub-optimal by Sri Lankan standards. The same Solargis dataset gives a PVOUT of 1,524 kWh/kWp/yr for a monofacial, fixed-tilt configuration, and the DutchBay pvlib producer independently reproduced 1,496 kWh/kWp — within two per cent of Solargis, which is a reassuring model-validation result but not a flattering resource number. A NASA POWER climatology cross-check of approximately 2,049 kWh/m²/yr for GHI broadly corroborates the order of magnitude. The practical consequence is a low capacity factor, examined in detail later, and it is no coincidence that the resource emerges in the sensitivity analysis as one of the two dominant drivers of project return. A wet-zone site starts the race several lengths back.

Taken together, the two locational facts — no developable land and a wet-zone resource — reinforce one another. The site is neither physically buildable at scale nor blessed with the irradiance that might otherwise justify creative siting effort. We assess the briefed location faithfully and in full, because that is the remit, but the reader should hold both caveats in mind throughout: the numbers that follow describe a plant at this point, and that point is, on the evidence, the wrong place on two independent counts. The most consequential single intervention identified anywhere in this report — relocation to a dry-zone north-eastern or south-eastern site for a yield uplift of some 15 to 20 per cent — flows directly from the resource picture set out here.

subheads.title: 3.1 Primary Datasets and the Bankable Reference
paragraphs: The solar-resource assessment for this site rests on two independent, primary data sources, supplemented by an in-house physical model. The first and principal reference is Solargis (version 2.2.68), accessed via the Global Solar Atlas, which reports a long-term annual Global Horizontal Irradiation (GHI) of 1,909 kWh/m² per year at the site coordinates of 6.8868°N, 79.9187°E. The accompanying irradiation components are a Direct Normal Irradiation (DNI) of 1,273 kWh/m² per year and a diffuse component of 940 kWh/m² per year, with a long-term average ambient temperature of 26.5°C and an optimum fixed-tilt angle of approximately 9°. Critically, Solargis translates this resource into a specific-yield estimate — the Photovoltaic Power Output (PVOUT) — of 1,524 kWh/kWp per year on a monofacial, fixed-tilt basis. It is this PVOUT figure, rather than the raw GHI, that drives the production and financial model, because it already embeds module orientation, temperature derating and standard system behaviour.

Solargis is adopted as the bankable reference dataset for this assessment, consistent with prevailing lender and development-finance-institution practice. The Solargis time series is satellite-derived, validated against ground-measurement networks, and carries the documented uncertainty bounds that lenders require for P50 and P90 bankability analysis. Its high diffuse fraction at this location — 940 kWh/m² per year against a GHI of 1,909 kWh/m² per year — is itself an important physical signal: roughly half of the incident resource arrives as diffuse rather than direct radiation, which is the expected fingerprint of a cloudy, humid, wet-zone climate and which constrains the achievable performance of any fixed-tilt array regardless of module quality. For the avoidance of doubt, we treat the Solargis monofacial PVOUT of 1,524 kWh/kWp per year as the anchor specific yield for the deterministic base case.

The second primary source is NASA POWER, drawn from its 2001-2020 climatology, which provides an independent cross-check on the resource. NASA POWER returns an annual GHI of approximately 2,049 kWh/m² per year at this location. The value of this second dataset lies not in displacing Solargis but in bounding it: two methodologically distinct satellite-and-reanalysis pipelines, processed by different institutions, can be compared to test whether the headline resource is an artefact of a single model. They are not. Both place the site firmly within the irradiation band expected for south-west Sri Lanka, and the convergence of two independent estimates materially strengthens confidence in the resource characterisation that underpins the financial conclusions.

subheads.title: 3.2 Inter-Dataset Spread and National Context
paragraphs: The two primary GHI estimates — Solargis at 1,909 kWh/m² per year and NASA POWER at approximately 2,049 kWh/m² per year — differ by roughly 7%. A spread of this magnitude is entirely normal for satellite-derived solar resource data and falls well within the combined uncertainty of the two methodologies; it should not be read as a discrepancy requiring reconciliation. The two products differ in their input satellite imagery, atmospheric and aerosol treatment, temporal coverage and spatial resolution, and a divergence of single-digit percentage points between them is the routine outcome of those methodological differences. For the purposes of this assessment we retain the more conservative Solargis figure as the modelling anchor, which has the effect of presenting the resource — and therefore the project economics — on a prudent rather than an optimistic footing. Were the higher NASA POWER value adopted instead, the yield would rise modestly, but as the financial sections demonstrate, no plausible resource within this 7% band moves the project toward viability.

Placing the site in its national context is essential to interpreting the resource correctly. The World Bank and Solargis national assessment for Sri Lanka reports a GHI range of 1,247 to 2,106 kWh/m² per year across the island. Against this national span, the site's Solargis GHI of 1,909 kWh/m² per year sits in the low-to-middle portion of the distribution — respectable in absolute terms, but materially below the island's best solar resource. This is a direct consequence of geography and climate: the site lies in Sri Lanka's south-west wet zone, which is the cloudiest, rainiest and among the lowest-irradiance regions of the country. The strongest solar resource in Sri Lanka is found in the dry zones of the north-east and south-east — areas such as Vavuniya, Pooneryn and Hambantota — where lower cloud cover and reduced atmospheric moisture lift both GHI and DNI well above the values recorded here. The implication is structural and should be stated plainly: this location is not a resource-optimal site for solar generation, and relocating to the dry zone would be expected to raise yield by 15 to 20%, the single largest lever available to the project.

It is also worth recording the practical siting reality that frames the entire resource discussion. The coordinates reverse-geocode to a dense urban and protected-wetland setting in the Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte and Battaramulla area, beside the Diyawanna Oya wetland and the national Parliament. There is realistically no contiguous 10 MW land parcel available at this location, and the resource assessment that follows should therefore be read as a site-representative characterisation of the south-west wet-zone climate rather than as confirmation of a deliverable project envelope at these exact coordinates.

subheads.title: 3.3 Independent Model Validation and the Bifacial Uplift
paragraphs: To avoid sole reliance on third-party data products, the resource was independently reproduced using the DutchBay pvlib production model, a physics-based simulation that takes the irradiation inputs and computes specific yield from first principles. The pvlib model returns a specific yield of 1,496 kWh/kWp per year on a monofacial, fixed-tilt basis, against the Solargis PVOUT of 1,524 kWh/kWp per year. The two figures agree to within 2%. This is a genuine model-validation result rather than a circular restatement of the same data: an independent toolchain, applied to the site inputs, converges on essentially the same specific yield as the commercial reference dataset. Such close agreement gives strong assurance that the production figures carried into the financial model are physically sound and free from systematic modelling error, and it allows the assessment to proceed on the Solargis anchor with confidence reinforced by an orthogonal method.

A point of methodological discipline must be made explicit regarding bifacial gain. The Solargis PVOUT of 1,524 kWh/kWp per year and the pvlib cross-check of 1,496 kWh/kWp per year are both monofacial figures — they describe the front-side energy yield of a conventional fixed-tilt array and make no allowance for rear-side generation. The bifacial uplift, estimated at approximately 5 to 10% for the recommended n-TOPCon and HJT module technologies, therefore sits on top of these monofacial baselines and must be added explicitly rather than assumed to be already embedded. Applying a representative bifacial gain of around 7% to the monofacial yield lifts the modelled capacity factor from 0.171 on a monofacial basis to 0.182-0.183 bifacial, corresponding to a year-one net energy of approximately 16.0 GWh and a plane-of-array irradiation of around 1,913 kWh/m² per year. Failing to treat the bifacial gain as an additive term would either double-count or omit it, so the convention adopted throughout this report is to state the monofacial PVOUT as the resource baseline and apply the bifacial uplift as a distinct, explicit adjustment.

Finally, the resource characterisation has been rendered into two spatial data products to support site comparison and any future relocation analysis: a national solar-resource map for Sri Lanka, which visualises the 1,247 to 2,106 kWh/m² per year GHI gradient and locates the site within the lower-resource south-west, and an accompanying GeoTIFF data product carrying the underlying gridded irradiation values. Together these deliverables make the central resource finding visually unambiguous — that the site, while adequately irradiated in absolute terms, is materially below the island's best solar resource, and that the dominant resource lever for the project is geographic relocation to the dry-zone north-east or south-east rather than any refinement of technology or system design at the present coordinates.

subheads.title: 4.1 Selection Criteria for a Hot, Humid, Salt-Laden Coastal-Wetland Environment
paragraphs: The module specification for this site is governed less by headline wattage than by the environmental stresses peculiar to its location. The project sits at 6.8868°N, 79.9187°E in Sri Lanka's south-west wet zone, immediately beside the Diyawanna Oya wetland, in a setting that is simultaneously hot, persistently humid, and exposed to salt-laden coastal air. With an average ambient temperature of 26.5°C and module cell temperatures running well above that under load, the dominant performance lever is the temperature coefficient of power: a lower (less negative) coefficient preserves more of the nameplate output through the heat of the day. A flat, mild-April-peak production profile means the plant operates near its thermal ceiling for much of the year, so every tenth of a percent per °C compounds across the 25-year project life.

The second criterion is bifaciality. A monofacial configuration at this site yields a capacity factor of 0.171; the assumed +7% bifacial gain lifts that to 0.182–0.183 and year-1 net energy to roughly 16.0 GWh, with a plane-of-array irradiance near 1,913 kWh/m²/yr. A higher and, critically, a datasheet-substantiated bifaciality factor is therefore directly load-bearing on the energy yield used throughout this assessment. The third and arguably decisive criterion is durability certification. A coastal, ammonia-rich wetland exposes modules to both salt mist and the nitrogenous compounds associated with wetland biology and agriculture; the relevant standards are IEC 61701 (salt-mist corrosion) and IEC 62716 (ammonia resistance). For a bankable, lender-financed asset, these cannot be inferred — they must be printed on the datasheet.

The fourth criterion is Tier-1 bankability and South-Asia supply assurance. A 25-year asset depends on the manufacturer surviving to honour its performance and product warranties, on a credible regional supply and service channel, and on a track record that satisfies a DFI or commercial lender's technical adviser. We have screened the market to a class of ≥600W bifacial n-type modules — the current frontier of mainstream utility supply — and assessed each shortlisted candidate against this combined lens of low temperature sensitivity, proven bifaciality, certified coastal durability, and bankability, rather than against datasheet wattage alone.

subheads.title: 4.2 Shortlist Assessment of the Four Candidate Modules
paragraphs: The Trina Vertex N TSM-NEG21C.20 is an n-TOPCon module rated at 720W with a bifaciality factor of 80±5% and a temperature coefficient of −0.29%/°C. Its distinguishing characteristic is that it is the only module on the shortlist datasheet-certified for both IEC 61701 salt-mist and IEC 62716 ammonia resistance — precisely the two stresses that define this coastal-wetland site — combined with the strongest South-Asia bankability profile. Its temperature coefficient is the least favourable of the four and its bifaciality is mid-range, but neither shortfall is large, and both are offset by certification that the others cannot match on paper.

The Risen Hyper-ion RSM132-8-...725BHDG is an n-HJT module rated at 700–725W with the best temperature coefficient of the group at −0.24%/°C and the highest indicative bifaciality at approximately 85–90%. The caveat is documentary rather than physical: 90% bifaciality is not printed on the datasheet, so for modelling and warranty purposes the 85% floor must be treated as the bankable figure. Heterojunction cells inherently favour high-temperature operation, which is attractive here, but the yield advantage this implies cannot be fully evidenced from the datasheet alone.

The Huasun Himalaya G12 HS-210-B132 is an n-HJT module rated at 700–720W with 85±5% bifaciality and a temperature coefficient of −0.26%/°C, supplied through an India-BIS channel that is advantageous for South-Asia logistics and customs. It pairs the thermal benefits of heterojunction with a credible regional supply route, making it a serious contender on resource performance and availability. The Astronergy ASTRO N7 Pro is an n-TOPCon module rated at 670W with the highest cell efficiency on the shortlist at 24.8% and a temperature coefficient of −0.26%/°C; launched in January 2026, it is the newest entrant, which is both its appeal (latest cell architecture) and its principal reservation (the shortest field and bankability track record of the four).

subheads.title: 4.3 Recommended Primary Module and the Bankability-over-Yield Trade-off
paragraphs: Our primary recommendation is the Trina Vertex N TSM-NEG21C.20 (720W, n-TOPCon). The reasoning turns on the central trade-off for this site: the two heterojunction candidates offer a temperature-coefficient edge (−0.24%/°C for Risen against Trina's −0.29%/°C) and a potential bifaciality edge that together imply roughly a 5% yield advantage, but that advantage is partly undocumented on the datasheet and, more importantly, is not the binding consideration. For a coastal-wetland asset, the binding consideration is certified survival in salt and ammonia over 25 years. Trina is the only shortlisted module to carry both IEC 61701 and IEC 62716 certification on its datasheet, and it pairs that with the best South-Asia bankability. A lender's technical adviser will weight a proven, certified, bankable module above an unevidenced single-digit yield premium, and so do we.

The alternates remain genuinely viable and each has a clear selection trigger. Choose Risen Hyper-ion where the thermal-performance edge is the priority and the bidder can obtain salt-mist and ammonia certification documentation to close the datasheet gap, treating 85% bifaciality as the contractual floor. Choose Huasun Himalaya where the India-BIS supply channel materially de-risks procurement logistics and lead time, with its −0.26%/°C coefficient and 85±5% bifaciality providing a balanced heterojunction option. Choose Astronergy ASTRO N7 Pro where maximum cell efficiency (24.8%) and the most current TOPCon architecture are valued and the buyer is comfortable with the shortest track record. In every case, equivalent coastal certification should be made a condition of supply.

Two procurement disciplines must be enforced. First, the exclusions: the REC Alpha Pure-RX (470W) falls below the ≥600W class threshold; Meyer Burger has exited PV manufacturing; and Akcome has halted production — none is bankable for a 25-year asset. Second, a specific LONGi caution: the LONGi Hi-MO 9 in this power class is an HPBC back-contact module, not a TOPCon device. Where a strict n-TOPCon specification is mandated — whether by lender, off-taker, or technical standard — the Hi-MO 9 must be excluded, and this distinction should be written explicitly into the technical schedule to prevent an inadvertent non-compliant substitution at tender. Finally, it must be stated plainly that this technology recommendation, while sound, does not alter the project's economics: the system-level energy model is module-agnostic, driven by capacity factor, plane-of-array irradiance, losses and degradation rather than by brand. The strongly negative project NPV and sub-WACC returns derive from the site's low wet-zone resource and the available tariffs, not from module choice — the procurement recommendation is sound and is not the problem.

subheads.title: 5.1 Rationale and Reproducibility
paragraphs: The energy yield underpinning this assessment is the single most influential input to the financial model, and our sensitivity analysis confirms it: capacity factor — the physical resource — is one of the two dominant drivers of project IRR, moving the unlevered return by roughly 1.7 percentage points across its credible band. A yield estimate that is opaque, irreproducible, or dependent on proprietary black-box software is therefore not lender-grade. For this reason we modelled production with a fully transparent, physics-based simulation built on the open-source pvlib library, in which every intermediate quantity — irradiance decomposition, plane-of-array transposition, cell temperature, DC and AC power — is exposed, auditable, and independently re-derivable from first principles. There are no hidden coefficients and no vendor-specific assumptions buried in the chain.

A physics-based approach is preferred here over a simple yield-per-kilowatt rule of thumb because it correctly propagates the site's specific climatic conditions — high ambient temperatures averaging 26.5°C, a high diffuse fraction characteristic of the cloudy south-west wet zone, and the bifacial and inverter-clipping behaviour of the chosen plant configuration — into the final figure rather than approximating them away. The model is configured to the actual plant design: 10 MWp of DC capacity, a fixed tilt of 9° (matching the site's optimum), a DC-to-AC ratio of 1.2, and a 14% system loss stack. Each of these is a deliberate, documented parameter rather than an embedded default.

Reproducibility is enforced by two design choices. First, the simulation runs against a single fixed reference year, so the same inputs always produce the same output and the result can be regenerated on demand by any reviewer. Second, the model depends on no external data files at run time; the meteorological boundary condition is a single measured annual figure rather than a large, mutable time-series archive that could drift between runs or between machines. This matters for an independent technical review, where a lender's engineer must be able to rebuild the yield number from the documented method alone. Notably, this physics-based pipeline independently reproduced an annual specific yield of 1,496 kWh/kWp against the Solargis benchmark of 1,524 kWh/kWp — agreement within 2% — which is itself a model-validation result and gives confidence that the simulation chain is correctly calibrated before any plant-specific gains are applied.

subheads.title: 5.2 The Seven-Step Simulation Chain
paragraphs: The simulation proceeds through seven sequential, physically motivated steps. Step one establishes a clear-sky irradiance baseline using the Ineichen–Perez clear-sky model, which provides the theoretical maximum global, direct, and diffuse irradiance for the site's latitude of 6.8868°N and longitude of 79.9187°E under cloudless conditions. This baseline is purely geometric and atmospheric; it encodes the sun's path and a clean-sky turbidity assumption but says nothing yet about the actual cloudiness of this particular wet-zone location. It serves as the physical scaffold onto which the measured resource is imposed.

Step two scales that clear-sky baseline to the measured resource so that the simulation reproduces the empirically observed annual global horizontal irradiance. We anchor to the Solargis (Global Solar Atlas v2.2.68) figure of 1,909 kWh/m²/yr of annual GHI — a primary, bankable source — cross-checked against NASA POWER's 2001–2020 climatology of approximately 2,049 kWh/m²/yr and sitting comfortably within the World Bank/Solargis national GHI range of 1,247 to 2,106 kWh/m²/yr. Scaling the clear-sky profile to the measured annual GHI ensures the model inherits the real cloud-loss signature of the south-west wet zone rather than an idealised clear-sky total, which would materially overstate yield in one of the island's cloudiest regions.

Step three decomposes the resulting global horizontal irradiance into its direct-normal (DNI) and diffuse-horizontal (DHI) components using the DISC model. This separation is essential because the direct and diffuse fractions strike a tilted array differently, and the wet-zone site is diffuse-rich: the Solargis data record an annual diffuse component of 940 kWh/m²/yr against a DNI of 1,273 kWh/m²/yr, so the diffuse fraction is far from negligible and must be handled explicitly rather than assumed. Step four then performs the plane-of-array transposition — projecting horizontal irradiance onto the 9° tilted module plane — using the anisotropic Hay–Davies model. We deliberately use Hay–Davies in preference to a simple isotropic transposition because the isotropic assumption treats diffuse sky radiance as uniform in all directions and systematically understates the circumsolar diffuse contribution near the solar disc. Hay–Davies resolves the diffuse component into circumsolar and isotropic parts, producing a more accurate and slightly higher POA estimate that is the lender-preferred standard for bankable yield assessments; the modelled annual POA irradiance is approximately 1,913 kWh/m²/yr.

Step five converts irradiance and weather into electrical output. Cell temperature is computed with the Faiman thermal model, which captures the wind- and irradiance-dependent heating of the module — a consequential effect at this site given the 26.5°C average ambient temperature and the negative temperature coefficients of the candidate modules — and DC power is then derived using the PVWatts DC model with the plant's array rating. Step six passes the DC output through the PVWatts inverter model under the specified 1.2 inverter loading ratio, so that the simulation correctly applies inverter conversion losses and clips DC power that exceeds the AC nameplate during peak hours; the 1.2 ILR is a deliberate over-sizing choice that lifts the AC capacity factor while accepting modest clipping at midday. Step seven applies the loss stack: a 14% aggregate system-loss allowance covering soiling, wiring, mismatch, availability and ancillary effects, followed by an explicit and separately stated +7% bifacial rear-side gain reflecting the bifacial n-TOPCon technology selected for the plant. Keeping the bifacial gain explicit, rather than folding it silently into the loss figure, lets a reviewer stress or remove it independently — appropriate discipline given that rear-side gain is the more uncertain element of the chain.

subheads.title: 5.3 Modelled Results and the Equatorial Profile
paragraphs: The seven-step chain yields a year-one net AC capacity factor of 0.182 to 0.183 once the +7% bifacial gain is applied (against a monofacial figure of 0.171), corresponding to roughly 16.0 GWh of net energy in the first year of operation and a specific yield of approximately 1,568 kWh/kWp. These figures are then carried into the financial model with a degradation rate of 0.5% per year over a 25-year project life and a 20-year PPA term. The modelled output sits in close and consistent relation to the independent benchmarks: the Solargis monofacial PVOUT of 1,524 kWh/kWp and the pvlib model's own monofacial reproduction of 1,496 kWh/kWp, with the higher headline specific yield attributable to the explicit bifacial uplift. The convergence of an independent open-source physics model with two external primary datasets is precisely the triangulation a lender's technical adviser looks for, and it gives the yield estimate a solid evidential footing even though the downstream economics are unattractive.

A distinctive and financially relevant feature of the modelled output is the flatness of the monthly production profile, a direct consequence of the site's near-equatorial latitude of 6.8868°N. Monthly energy varies only between roughly 1.25 and 1.41 GWh, with a mild peak in April and a shallow trough in November — a far tighter seasonal spread than is seen at higher-latitude solar sites, where winter output can fall to a fraction of the summer peak. From a project-finance perspective this equatorial flatness is a genuine structural advantage: it produces a stable, predictable monthly revenue stream, smooths debt-service coverage across the year, and removes the seasonal cash-flow troughs that can force conservative debt sizing or larger liquidity reserves elsewhere. The cash-flow stability does not rescue the underlying economics — the binding problem is the unlevered asset return under the available tariffs, not the shape of the production calendar — but it is a real and creditworthy attribute of the resource that this methodology surfaces clearly and that would carry weight under any future, better-sited configuration.

subheads.title: 6.1 Engine, Revenue and Cash-Flow Construction
paragraphs: This assessment was run through the DutchBay v14 project-finance engine — the same code path that underpins the platform's wind portfolio — rather than a bespoke spreadsheet, so that the solar case inherits a tested, version-controlled cash-flow architecture and is directly comparable with the firm's other renewable mandates. The engine constructs an annual cash-flow vector over the full 25-year project life, against a 20-year power-purchase agreement, and treats the asset as a single 10 MW (ac) solar PV plant. Net generation is derived from the DutchBay pvlib producer at a year-one figure of approximately 16.0 GWh, reflecting a capacity factor of 0.182 to 0.183 under the bifacial-gain assumption, and is then degraded at 0.5% per year to capture panel ageing across the operating period. Using the engine common to the wind book is itself a control: it means the unusual result reported here is a property of the solar economics, not of an untested model.

Revenue in each period is the product of net generation and the applicable fixed PPA tariff. The model is run under two tariff regimes — the SLSEA standardised feed-in tariff of LKR 14.46/kWh for plants above 1 MW, which is the most plausible regulatory outcome for a standalone 10 MW plant following the June 2025 reduction, and a competitive USD-linked PPA at USc 8.00/kWh modelled as a fixed LKR 26.70/kWh struck at signing FX. Because both tariffs are fixed in rupee terms, revenue does not escalate with inflation, which is a deliberately conservative treatment given that a material part of the cost base is denominated in or indexed to US dollars. The competitive tariff is, in effect, the best-achievable price benchmarked to the Siyambalanduwa 100 MW award, and is only realistically accessible through a larger competitive tender rather than to a standalone sub-10 MW project. Running the two regimes side by side allows the report to separate the regulatory question of price from the engineering question of yield.

From revenue the engine builds cash flow available for debt service by deducting operating expenditure of USD 130,000 per year (USD 13/kW-yr) and the applicable statutory deductions. Sri Lankan corporate income tax is applied at {tax}, with a {lcf_years}-year tax-loss carry-forward and five-year straight-line depreciation of the plant share of capex (twenty years for civil works) modelled so that the shield is recognised in the periods in which it genuinely arises rather than assumed away. A further {haircut} haircut is then applied to CFADS as a risk reserve; this is a conservative provision even for a low-variability technology such as solar, and it deliberately errs on the side of caution in sizing the cash available to lenders. The resulting CFADS profile is the quantity on which all debt-sizing and coverage tests are subsequently performed, so the prudence embedded here flows through the whole financing analysis.

subheads.title: 6.2 Debt Sizing, DSCR Sculpting and the WACC
paragraphs: A central methodological point is that the engine sizes the debt rather than assuming it. Two sizing disciplines are run in parallel. The first is a fixed-ratio approach at {gearing} gearing, used as the base structure for comparability across the firm's mandates. The second is dual-DSCR sculpting, in which the engine solves for the debt quantum that the CFADS profile can actually support at a target minimum debt-service-coverage ratio, subject to a covenant floor of 1.30×. Debt is structured across three tranches — an LKR tranche at {lkr_rate} (up to {lkr_max} of the debt), a DFI tranche at {dfi_rate} (up to {dfi_max}) and a USD commercial tranche at {usd_rate} (at least {usd_min}) — over a {tenor}-year tenor with {io_years} interest-only years, after a {constr_years}-year construction period. In the sculpted runs the engine reports the achieved DSCR profile alongside the sized debt, so the coverage outcome is an output of the model, not an input to it.

The DSCR work is the key analytical follow-up, because it isolates what is and is not binding. Sweeping the minimum-DSCR target from {dscr_lo}× to {dscr_hi}× shows that the unlevered project IRR is invariant at {dscr_proj_irr}, with project NPV unchanged at {dscr_proj_npv}: the DSCR is a financing-structure parameter, not a constraint on the asset's underlying return. A lower target draws more debt — gearing of {dscr_gear_lo} at {dscr_lo}× against {dscr_gear_hi} at {dscr_hi}×. Comparing the two ends of the band, equity IRR is lower at the permissive end ({dscr_eq_lo} against {dscr_eq_hi}), the signature of negative carry, while equity NPV is marginally higher there ({dscr_eqnpv_lo} against {dscr_eqnpv_hi}), so the optimisation, which ranks on equity NPV, selects {dscr_best}×. Neither measure moves smoothly between the ends: below the {dscr_cov}× lock-up threshold the equity waterfall traps every distribution until the debt is repaid, so both measures step at {dscr_cov}× (Section 9). Neither measure comes near viability at any target. The binding constraint is the unlevered asset return itself, a finding that the sculpting machinery makes explicit rather than obscures.

Project cash flows are discounted at the scenario's declared project discount rate of {disc}. Equity cash flows are discounted at the equity waterfall's own rate of {eq_npv_disc}, a flat rate that is not relevered as gearing changes and that sits below the scenario's declared {eq_disc} equity hurdle. The scenario also carries a CAPM cost-of-capital block, which builds a nominal WACC of {wacc_built} from a Sri Lankan risk-free rate, a relevered beta and its own assumptions of a {wacc_kd} cost of debt at {wacc_gear} gearing; it does not read the tranche terms above. That block is not set to drive discounting, so the engine reports the {wacc_built} WACC for information only. Discounting at the built WACC would deepen every project NPV in this report. The engine reports both the unlevered project IRR and NPV — the return to the asset before financing — and the levered equity IRR and NPV, computed from a cash-flow vector that is construction-lag-correct, so that the construction period and the timing of first generation are reflected in the discounting rather than smeared across the early years. Keeping the project and equity views distinct is what allows the model to show that the shortfall originates in the asset. It is this separation that underwrites the report's conclusion that no financing structure can repair a return that is deficient before any debt is layered on.

subheads.title: 6.3 Foreign-Exchange Treatment
paragraphs: The model is run with the rupee as the primary currency and uses a starting exchange rate of LKR 333.79 per US dollar. The dollar-denominated cost base — principally the USD 12.0M capital expenditure (USD 1,200/kW) and the USD 130,000 per year of operating expenditure — is escalated for currency risk at {fx_depr} per year of LKR depreciation, so that the rupee cost of servicing those items rises over the life of the plant. This is the realistic direction of travel for a small open economy with a persistent external deficit, and excluding it would flatter the economics. Crucially, the revenue side is held fixed in rupee terms under both tariff regimes, including the competitive PPA, which is struck as a fixed LKR 26.70/kWh at signing FX rather than being re-translated each year. The combination — depreciating rupee costs against a flat rupee tariff — is deliberately conservative and means the FX assumptions, if anything, understate rather than overstate the difficulty the project faces. The robustness of the negative verdict across the deterministic, Monte Carlo, sensitivity and optimisation lenses cannot therefore be attributed to an aggressive currency stance; it survives precisely because the currency treatment was chosen to be unflattering to the costs and generous to the tariff.

subheads.title: 7.1 Deterministic Results Across the Two Tariff Regimes
paragraphs: The deterministic base case was run under the two tariff regimes that a standalone 10 MW solar plant could realistically secure, and neither produces a viable outcome. Under the base / likely regulatory regime — the SLSEA standardised feed-in tariff of LKR {fit_lkr}/kWh applicable to plants above 1 MW, reduced in June 2025 — the project returns a project IRR of {fit_irr} and a project NPV of {fit_npv} at the {disc} discount rate. A negative IRR is not a marginal shortfall against the cost of capital; it means the undiscounted lifetime cash flows do not return the initial capital outlay at all. No discount rate solves the equity cash flows in this case, so the equity IRR is undefined. The accompanying minimum DSCR of {fit_dscr} tells the same story from the lender's seat: in the worst covenant period the cash available for debt service covers only {fit_dscr_pct} of the scheduled obligation, so the asset cannot support standard project-finance debt under this tariff on any sensible sizing.

The competitive / best-achievable regime improves the picture but does not rescue it. Modelling a competitive USD PPA at USc {comp_usc}/kWh — the Siyambalanduwa 100 MW benchmark, struck here as a fixed LKR {comp_lkr}/kWh at signing FX — lifts the project IRR to {comp_irr} and narrows the project NPV to {comp_npv}. The minimum DSCR rises to {comp_dscr} at {gearing} gearing, still far below the 1.30× covenant: the plant generates only {comp_dscr_pct} of the cash needed to service debt at that leverage. A project IRR of {comp_irr} against the {disc} discount rate leaves a gap of {gap_pp} percentage points, and at standard gearing the asset cannot service its debt: the sponsor funds {comp_cure} of debt service over the tenor and the equity receives only {comp_eq_dist} in distributions. The equity IRR of {comp_eq_irr} on those cash flows carries little information, and equity NPV is the measure to read. It is worth stating plainly that this competitive tariff is itself only accessible through a larger competitive tender, not to a standalone 10 MW scheme, so the more favourable of the two regimes is also the less attainable one for the project as scoped.

The contrast between the two regimes is instructive but does not alter the verdict. Moving from the rupee FiT to the competitive USD PPA improves the project IRR by {irr_lift_pp} percentage points and the project NPV by {npv_lift}, which confirms that tariff is a powerful lever — but it is a lever that, even pulled to its best realistic setting, leaves the project NPV strongly negative and the IRR far short of the cost of capital. In both regimes the conclusion is identical: the project is not viable, and the project NPV is strongly negative. The difference between the two is the difference between a poor outcome and a slightly less poor one, not between failure and success.

subheads.title: 7.2 Reading the Metrics — Project IRR for Viability, DSCR for Debt Capacity
paragraphs: Two distinct metrics carry the analysis, and it is important to be clear about what each measures. The project (unlevered) IRR is the cleanest measure of viability because it strips out financing structure entirely: it reflects only the asset's own cash-generating capacity against its capital cost, independent of how the project is funded. This is why the project IRR is invariant to gearing and to the DSCR target in the sculpting analysis — it answers the prior question of whether the underlying asset earns its keep before any debt is layered on. At {fit_irr} under the FiT and {comp_irr} under the competitive PPA, both far below the {disc} discount rate, the project IRR delivers an unambiguous reading: the asset does not, on this resource and at these tariffs, generate a return that justifies the capital deployed. It is the figure on which the go / no-go decision properly rests.

The minimum DSCR, by contrast, is a debt-capacity measure: it asks how much of the scheduled debt service the project's cash flows can actually cover in its tightest period, and it is therefore a financing-structure parameter rather than a property of the asset's return. The base-case minimum DSCRs of {fit_dscr} under the FiT and {comp_dscr} under the competitive PPA sit far beneath the 1.30× covenant, signalling that at {gearing} gearing the plant is structurally unable to meet lender protections. Crucially, a weak DSCR can in principle be addressed by de-levering — reducing the debt quantum until coverage is restored — whereas a weak project IRR cannot be financed away. Reading the two metrics together shows that the problem here is not merely an over-geared capital structure that sculpting could repair; it is that the unlevered asset return itself is inadequate, and the DSCR shortfall is a downstream symptom of that, not an independent constraint. This distinction matters because it directs attention to the right lever: the resource and the tariff, not the debt sizing.

subheads.title: 7.3 Breakeven — How Far the Tariff Would Have to Move
paragraphs: The breakeven analysis quantifies precisely how large the gap is by solving for the tariff each test would require. To meet the 1.30× minimum-DSCR covenant at {gearing} gearing — the floor this scenario applies to debt sizing — the plant needs a tariff of approximately LKR {be_dscr_lkr}/kWh, equivalent to about USc {be_dscr_usc}/kWh. To push the project IRR up to the {disc} discount rate, so that the asset clears its cost of capital, the required tariff rises further to approximately LKR {be_irr_lkr}/kWh, or about USc {be_irr_usc}/kWh. These are not incremental adjustments. The DSCR-breakeven tariff is roughly {be_dscr_x_fit}× the prevailing LKR {fit_lkr} FiT, and the IRR-breakeven tariff is roughly {be_irr_x_comp}× the competitive USc {comp_usc} PPA. No tariff available to this project — neither the standardised rupee FiT nor the best-achievable competitive USD PPA — comes anywhere close to either threshold.

It is tempting to look to capital cost as the alternative route to breakeven, and the sensitivity work confirms that capex is a genuine lever: a ±10% change in capex (USD 1,080–1,320/kW) moves project IRR across a band of {t_capex_pp} percentage points, ranking behind only capacity factor and tariff among the drivers. The base case already adopts USD 1,200/kW (USD 12.0M total), which sits within the verified Sri Lankan utility-PV range of 1,100–1,350/kW and is consistent with the Siyambalanduwa implied figure of around 1,320/kW. Driving capex down towards the global frontier of 700–900/kW would help materially, but the arithmetic is decisive: a lever worth {t_capex_pp} percentage points of project IRR across that band cannot, on its own, close a gap that requires the tariff to rise roughly {be_irr_x_comp}-fold from the competitive price. The breakeven analysis therefore reinforces the central finding that the binding constraint is the combination of a low-irradiance wet-zone resource and the available tariffs, and that no single financing or cost lever, applied alone, brings this asset to viability.

subheads.title: 8.1 Monte Carlo Simulation: A Robustly Sub-Economic Distribution
paragraphs: To establish whether the deterministic verdict is an artefact of single-point assumptions, we subjected the model to a {mc_n}-trial Monte Carlo simulation using Latin-Hypercube sampling under a fixed seed of 123. Latin-Hypercube sampling stratifies each input across its full probability range, ensuring the sampled space is covered far more evenly than crude random draws and delivering stable distributional statistics at a modest trial count. We varied the three economically material inputs across evidence-based ranges: capacity factor as a normal distribution spanning 0.165 to 0.199 (capturing resource and bifacial-gain uncertainty), capex as a triangular distribution from USD 1,050 to 1,350 per kW (reflecting the verified Sri Lankan utility-PV band), and opex as a uniform distribution from USD 110,000 to 160,000 per year, all at the competitive tariff. Common random numbers were applied as a variance-reduction technique, so that differences between trials reflect the sampled inputs rather than sampling noise. The simulation completed with {mc_failed} failed trials.

The resulting distribution of project IRR is tightly clustered and uniformly sub-economic. The tenth, fiftieth and ninetieth percentiles land at {mc_p10}, {mc_p50} and {mc_p90} respectively, with a mean of {mc_mean} — a narrow span across the full range of plausible inputs. {mc_p_neg} of trials return a negative project IRR, and the best single trial reaches only {mc_best}. More tellingly, {mc_reach} of the {mc_n} trials reach the {disc} discount rate. The asset does not merely underperform its cost of capital on a central estimate; it fails to clear that hurdle under any combination of favourable resource, capex and opex draws within the sampled space. The narrowness of the distribution is itself a finding: because the dominant drivers are bounded by their physical and market realities, there is no plausible upside scenario in which the economics turn bankable.

The equity distribution is materially worse than the project distribution, as one would expect from an asset whose unlevered return sits below its cost of debt. In {eq_undefined} of the {mc_n} trials no discount rate solves the equity cash flows at all, so the equity IRR is undefined. In the {eq_defined} trials where it is defined, the median equity IRR is {eq_p50}, and {eq_p_neg} of them are negative. As in the deterministic case (Section 7.1), these IRRs are computed on cash flows dominated by the initial equity outlay and sponsor-funded debt service, so they say little beyond their sign. This is the quantitative signature of negative carry: layering debt onto an asset that cannot earn its financing cost transfers value away from equity rather than amplifying it. Taken together, the Monte Carlo results confirm that the deterministic conclusion is not a fragile, single-input artefact but a robust property of the asset under this resource, cost and tariff regime. The probabilistic lens widens the analysis without rescuing the investment case.

subheads.title: 8.2 One-Way Sensitivity: Resource and Tariff Dominate
paragraphs: To identify which assumptions most influence the outcome, we constructed a one-way tornado analysis on project IRR at the competitive tariff, flexing each input independently while holding the others at base case. The structure of the tornado is itself informative and serves as an internal validation of the model. The two dominant drivers are capacity factor — the underlying solar resource — and tariff, each flexed by ±10% and each moving project IRR across a band of {t_cf_pp} and {t_tariff_pp} percentage points respectively. The two are equal by construction, because revenue is the product of energy and price. That these two sit at the top is intuitive and correct: for a renewable asset with no fuel cost, the unlevered return is fundamentally a function of how much energy the site yields and the price at which that energy is sold. The pre-eminence of capacity factor is also a direct quantitative expression of the siting problem, since the south-west wet zone offers among the lowest irradiance on the island.

CAPEX is the next most influential input, moving project IRR across a band of {t_capex_pp} percentage points for a ±10% change — significant, but secondary to the resource and the price of output. Opex (±15%) and the corporate tax rate (±20%) are second-order, at {t_opex_pp} and {t_tax_pp} percentage points respectively; the {tax} corporate income tax, mitigated by tax-loss carry-forward and accelerated depreciation, does little to reorder the conclusion, and the modest opex envelope of a low-maintenance solar asset has limited leverage. Critically, debt tenor has zero effect on the unlevered project IRR ({t_tenor_pp} points). This is not an oversight but a correct internal validation: the project IRR is, by construction, a measure of the asset's return independent of how it is financed, so a financing-structure parameter such as tenor must leave it untouched. The fact that the model behaves this way gives confidence that the engine is correctly separating asset performance from capital structure.

The practical implication of the tornado is that the levers capable of changing the verdict are precisely the ones tied to the physical asset and its revenue, not its financial engineering. Improving the capacity factor — which in practice means relocating to a higher-irradiance dry-zone site — and securing a stronger tariff are the only single-variable moves with meaningful traction, and even those, at {t_cf_pp} percentage points each across a ±10% band, are individually insufficient to close the {gap_pp}-point gap between the base project IRR of {comp_irr} and the {disc} discount rate. The tornado therefore reinforces a recurring theme of this assessment: the problem is structural and located in the asset's fundamentals, and no amount of tuning the second-order or financing inputs reaches a bankable result.

subheads.title: 8.3 Capital-Structure Optimisation: The Limits of Leverage
paragraphs: The final lens is an optimisation over capital structure under fixed sizing, seeking the gearing between {opt_lo} and {opt_hi} that maximises equity NPV subject to a minimum per-period DSCR of 1.30x. The optimiser ranks on equity NPV rather than equity IRR because an IRR can rank options wrongly. {eq_sign_sentence} The IRR is undefined under the feed-in tariff and in {eq_undefined} of the {mc_n} Monte Carlo trials, and it misranks covenant settings that shift distributions in time (Section 9). The result is stark: no gearing in the band meets the covenant. The minimum per-period DSCR is {opt_dscr_lo} even at {opt_lo} gearing and falls to {opt_dscr_hi} at {opt_hi}, so the cash flows cannot carry even the least-levered structure tested. Across the band, equity NPV rises with leverage, from {opt_npv_lo} at {opt_lo} to {opt_npv_hi} at {opt_hi}, while equity IRR falls from {opt_eq_lo} to {opt_eq_hi}; every point remains deeply negative and outside the covenant.

The rise in equity NPV is not value that the asset creates. It comes from two features of the financing. First, in dollar terms every tranche costs less than the flat {eq_npv_disc} rate at which the equity cash flows are discounted: {dfi_rate} for the DFI tranche and {usd_rate} for the USD tranche, and the {lkr_rate} LKR rate is the USD rate plus the scenario's {fx_depr} expected depreciation, so it costs about the same as the USD tranche once the rupee's fall is allowed for. That {eq_npv_disc} rate is not relevered as gearing rises. Second, at fixed gearing the asset cannot cover its debt service, so the sponsor funds the shortfall: sponsor cures rise from {opt_cure_lo} at {opt_lo} gearing to {opt_cure_hi} at {opt_hi}. Replacing equity with cheaper debt that the sponsor then services lifts the NPV at a flat rate without making the project any better. Even the sculpted sizing in Section 9, at a permissive {dscr_lo}× target, reaches only {dscr_gear_lo} gearing. The genuinely binding constraint is the unlevered asset return itself, a point the separate DSCR investigation confirms by showing the project IRR invariant at {dscr_proj_irr} regardless of how the financing is sculpted.

Across all three probabilistic and analytical lenses — the Monte Carlo distribution, the sensitivity tornado and the capital-structure optimisation — the conclusion converges and holds. The simulation finds no path to the cost of capital across {mc_n} trials; the tornado locates the binding levers in the physical resource and tariff rather than in any financing parameter; and the optimisation demonstrates that no gearing choice can rescue an asset whose fundamentals do not clear its hurdle rate. The robustness of the verdict is not a matter of a single conservative assumption but the agreement of multiple independent analytical perspectives, all pointing to the same structural conclusion: the limiting factor is the asset's unlevered economics at this site and under these tariffs, and that cannot be financed away.

dscr.title: 9. Is the 1.30x DSCR Covenant Itself Limiting?

subheads.title: The Question, and How We Made the Covenant a Live Lever
paragraphs: A standard objection to any "not viable" verdict on a leveraged infrastructure asset is that the result may be an artefact of an over-cautious covenant rather than a feature of the underlying economics. The minimum debt-service cover ratio (DSCR) of 1.30× assumed throughout this assessment is precisely the sort of parameter that invites this challenge: tighten it and you starve the structure of debt; loosen it and you might, in principle, admit enough cheap leverage to rescue equity returns. Because the headline conclusion rests in part on the asset's inability to carry standard project-finance debt, it is right to interrogate whether the 1.30× figure is itself doing the damage. This section sets out a dedicated investigation into exactly that question, and the answer is unambiguous: the covenant is not the binding constraint.

Before turning to the mechanics, it is worth distinguishing two quite different roles the DSCR plays, because conflating them is the source of most confusion. In a fixed-sizing structure, debt is set by a chosen gearing ratio and the DSCR is simply an achieved outcome — a diagnostic readout of how comfortably cash flow available for debt service (CFADS) covers the scheduled obligation. In a sculpted-sizing structure, the DSCR is instead the sizing target: debt is sized backwards from the cash flows so that cover lands on the chosen ratio in each period, making the covenant an active input that genuinely determines how much leverage the asset can support. Under the fixed-ratio base case the achieved cover is alarmingly thin — a minimum DSCR of {fit_dscr} under the rupee feed-in tariff and {comp_dscr} under the competitive tariff at {gearing} gearing — meaning only {fit_dscr_pct} to {comp_dscr_pct} of debt service is covered, and standard debt cannot be serviced at all. But an achieved DSCR cannot tell us whether the target covenant is the limiting factor, because in that mode the target does nothing.

To test the target properly, we therefore switched the scenario to DSCR-sculpted sizing, where the minimum-DSCR figure is a live lever rather than a passive readout, and then swept that target across a wide band — from a permissive {dscr_lo}× up to a demanding {dscr_hi}× — running each point through the full optimisation routine. This design lets the model re-size the debt at every step: a lower target admits more debt and higher gearing, while a higher target forces deleveraging. If the 1.30× covenant were genuinely the obstacle, we would expect to see returns improve materially as the target is relaxed towards {dscr_lo}×. They do not.

subheads.title: Two Findings: Invariant Asset Return, and Negative Carry on the Debt
paragraphs: The first finding is the more fundamental of the two, and it disposes of the question directly. Across the entire {dscr_lo}× to {dscr_hi}× sweep, the unlevered project IRR is invariant at {dscr_proj_irr}, and the project NPV is likewise unchanged at {dscr_proj_npv}. This is exactly as it should be: the DSCR governs how the asset's cash flows are sliced between lenders and equity, but it cannot conjure additional cash from the plant. The unlevered return is a property of the asset — the resource, the tariff, the capex and the opex — and is wholly indifferent to the financing wrapper placed around it. The DSCR is therefore a financing-structure parameter, not a constraint on the asset's return. Whatever is wrong with this project at {dscr_proj_irr} against the {disc} discount rate is wrong at the level of the asset itself, and no covenant setting touches it.

The second finding concerns what happens to the equity as the target moves. Relaxing the target to {dscr_lo}× admits more debt, but not much: gearing rises only to {dscr_gear_lo}, against {dscr_gear_hi} at {dscr_hi}×. Between the two ends of the band, equity IRR is lower at the permissive end, {dscr_eq_lo} at {dscr_lo}× against {dscr_eq_hi} at {dscr_hi}×. That is the signature of negative carry: the unlevered asset earns only {dscr_proj_irr}, so additional borrowing dilutes rather than enhances the equity return. Equity NPV at the {eq_npv_disc} equity discount rate is marginally higher at the permissive end ({dscr_eqnpv_lo} against {dscr_eqnpv_hi}), for the financing-rate reason set out in Section 8.3. Neither measure moves smoothly between the ends. Below the {dscr_cov}× lock-up threshold, the equity waterfall traps every distribution for {dscr_lock_years} years and releases it only when the debt is repaid. Relaxing the target from {dscr_cov}× to {dscr_below}× therefore raises equity IRR, from {dscr_eq_cov} to {dscr_eq_below}, but lowers equity NPV, from {dscr_eqnpv_cov} to {dscr_eqnpv_below}; equity NPV is lowest at {dscr_dip}× ({dscr_eqnpv_dip}). This is a clean example of why the platform ranks on NPV: an IRR solved at a negative rate gives extra weight to the later, larger release that the lock-up produces, while the NPV discounts it. The optimisation selects {dscr_best}×, but its advantage over {dscr_cov}× is only {dscr_best_margin}. That the measures disagree, and that the NPV difference across the whole band is small, is precisely what one would not observe if the covenant were the thing holding returns back.

Read together, these two results settle the matter. The unlevered return is invariant, so the covenant cannot be improving or harming the asset; and within the financing layer, the target moves equity NPV by no more than {dscr_npv_span} across the whole band, and not in one direction, leaving the equity deeply negative on both measures. There is therefore no setting of the DSCR target — permissive or demanding — that converts this project into a viable one. The lever simply has no purchase on the problem.

subheads.title: Conclusion: The Covenant Is Not the Constraint
paragraphs: The 1.30× minimum-DSCR covenant is not the binding constraint on this project. The binding constraint is the unlevered asset return of {dscr_proj_irr}, which sits far below the {disc} discount rate and which no financing structure can repair. Relaxing the covenant would admit little additional debt — gearing moves only between {dscr_gear_hi} and {dscr_gear_lo} across the whole band tested — and would move the equity NPV by no more than {dscr_npv_span}, in no consistent direction. It would not unlock value in any meaningful sense, and a lender reviewing this file should draw no comfort from the idea that loosening it might. This is consistent with the wider evidence in this report, where the dominant drivers of project IRR are the resource (capacity factor) and the tariff, while financing-side parameters such as debt tenor have zero effect on the unlevered return — a correct internal validation that the asset's problem is operational and commercial, not structural.

One practical caveat on the covenant deserves to be stated for completeness, because it bears on equity timing rather than headline viability. In any region where achieved cover falls below the covenant — and under fixed-ratio gearing the base case breaches comfortably, with minimum DSCRs of {fit_dscr} and {comp_dscr} — the standard lock-up provisions in a project-finance facility would trap cash and suspend distributions to equity until cover is restored, and the sponsor would have to fund the shortfall in debt service. For an asset whose cover is structurally thin rather than transiently impaired, this means equity would face an indefinite distribution lock-up, deferring or extinguishing returns that are already deeply negative on a discounted basis. This compounds the equity case but does not alter it: the lock-up is a symptom of the same root cause, an unlevered return that cannot service standard debt, and it reinforces rather than qualifies the recommendation. The covenant investigation thus closes the door on the most plausible "it's just the financing" rebuttal — the financing is not the problem, the asset is.

discussion.title: 10. Discussion — What Would Change the Verdict

subheads.title: Three Compounding Structural Factors
paragraphs: The verdict reached in the preceding sections — that a standalone 10 MW solar plant at this site is not viable under any available commercial terms — is not the product of a single adverse assumption but of three structural factors that compound on one another. The first is the resource. The site sits in Sri Lanka's south-west wet zone, the cloudiest, rainiest and among the lowest-irradiance regions of the island, delivering a Solargis PVOUT of 1,524 kWh/kWp/yr and a modelled bifacial capacity factor of only 0.182-0.183. The best solar resource on the island lies in the dry north-east and south-east — Vavuniya, Pooneryn, Hambantota — not here. The second factor is revenue: the most plausible regulatory outcome is the SLSEA standardised feed-in tariff of LKR {fit_lkr}/kWh for plants above 1 MW, a rupee-denominated price that is both low in real terms and exposed to currency erosion. The third is the cost of capital and capex: a {disc} discount rate, against which the scenario's own CAPM block builds a higher {wacc_built} WACC, and a USD 12.0M build (USD 1,200/kW) that, while consistent with the verified Sri Lankan utility-PV range of 1,100-1,350/kW, sits well above the global frontier of 700-900/kW.

These three factors interact rather than simply adding together. A mediocre resource produces too little energy; a low rupee tariff prices that energy too cheaply; and a high cost of capital discounts the resulting cash flows too harshly. The consequence is a negative unlevered return — project IRR of {fit_irr} under the feed-in tariff and {comp_irr} under the best-achievable competitive case, against a {disc} discount rate in both regimes. The breakeven analysis quantifies the size of the gap precisely: the plant needs around LKR {be_dscr_lkr}/kWh (roughly USc {be_dscr_usc}) merely to meet the 1.30× minimum-DSCR covenant, and around LKR {be_irr_lkr}/kWh (roughly USc {be_irr_usc}) for the project IRR to reach the discount rate. That is approximately {be_dscr_x_fit}× the feed-in tariff for the covenant alone, and roughly {be_irr_x_comp}× the competitive USc {comp_usc} tariff for the return. No available tariff comes close, and this is the lens through which every potential lever must be judged: each must be capable of moving the economics by a margin measured in multiples, not percentage points.

subheads.title: The Levers, in Order of Power
paragraphs: The single largest lever is the site itself. Relocating to a dry-zone site in the north-east or south-east would add an estimated 15-20% to yield, directly attacking the weakest of the three structural factors. The sensitivity analysis confirms why this matters most: capacity factor — the resource — is one of the two dominant drivers in the one-way tornado, moving project IRR across a band of {t_cf_pp} percentage points for a ±10% change, and the resource lever is the only one that improves the asset's fundamental energy yield rather than merely re-pricing or re-financing it. A better site also tends to come with land that genuinely exists at the required scale, which this location does not. It is worth restating plainly that the coordinates reverse-geocode to Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte — the Parliament Approach, Pita Kotte East and Battaramulla area of Colombo District — a dense urban and protected-wetland setting beside the Diyawanna Oya. There is realistically no 10 MW of contiguous developable land here at all, so relocation is not merely the most powerful lever but, in this instance, a precondition for the project to exist.

The second lever is harder revenue. The competitive USD PPA benchmark of USc {comp_usc}/kWh — the Siyambalanduwa 100 MW precedent, modelled here as a fixed LKR {comp_lkr}/kWh struck at signing FX — lifts the project IRR from {fit_irr} to {comp_irr} and narrows the NPV shortfall from {fit_npv} to {comp_npv}. Tariff is the joint-dominant driver in the tornado, moving project IRR across a band of {t_tariff_pp} percentage points, on a par with the resource. But this lever is only accessible at scale: the CEB no longer runs USD competitive bids for sub-10 MW projects, so a standalone 10 MW most plausibly receives the rupee feed-in tariff and nothing better. Securing the USc {comp_usc} price therefore requires bundling into a larger competitively-tendered programme, which would also bring capex economies of scale. A genuinely USD-indexed contract carries a second benefit beyond the headline price: it removes the foreign-exchange drag embedded in any LKR-fixed tariff, under which {fx_depr} a year of rupee depreciation steadily erodes the USD value of revenue against largely USD-linked costs.

The third lever is cheaper capital and cheaper capex. On the financing side, blending in more DFI or concessional debt would displace the {lkr_rate} LKR tranche, the most expensive of the three in nominal rupee terms ({dfi_rate} DFI and {usd_rate} USD being the others; on the scenario's own basis the LKR rate is the USD rate plus expected depreciation), and would lower the cost of the debt the project actually carries. On the construction side, a competitive EPC tender pushing the USD 1,200/kW build toward the global frontier of 700-900/kW would attack capex directly — the third-ranked driver in the tornado, at {t_capex_pp} percentage points of project IRR for a ±10% change. It is important to be clear about what this lever cannot do. The DSCR investigation showed that the unlevered project IRR is invariant at {dscr_proj_irr} as the minimum-DSCR target is swept from {dscr_lo}× to {dscr_hi}×, and that leverage produces negative carry — equity IRR falls as gearing rises; equity NPV rises, but only through the financing-rate spread and sponsor-funded debt service described in Section 8.3, and it stays deeply negative. Re-financing therefore cannot rescue a return problem that originates in the asset itself; only cheaper capex genuinely improves the underlying economics, and even that is a {t_capex_pp}-point lever against a gap measured in multiples.

subheads.title: Modelling Conservatisms and the Land Reality
paragraphs: A fair reading of this assessment must acknowledge where the model has been deliberately conservative, and then ask whether relaxing those conservatisms could close the gap. Three are worth naming. First, the CFADS risk haircut is set at {haircut}, a figure typical of wind projects with their higher inter-annual variability rather than of low-variability solar; a lighter haircut would be defensible. Second, the headline tariffs are modelled as LKR-fixed, which loads the full burden of {fx_depr} a year of rupee depreciation onto revenue while costs remain largely USD-linked — a genuine drag that a USD-indexed contract would remove. Third, no single-axis tracking uplift has been credited; the production rests on a fixed-tilt configuration at the optimum 9°.

None of these conservatisms, individually, closes a gap of this magnitude. The breakeven requirement is a tariff of roughly LKR {be_dscr_lkr}-{be_irr_lkr}/kWh against a feed-in tariff of LKR {fit_lkr} and a competitive price of USc {comp_usc} — a shortfall of {be_dscr_x_comp} to {be_irr_x_fit} times. Trimming a {haircut} haircut to a solar-appropriate level, removing FX drag, or adding a tracking uplift each moves the needle by a fraction of one such multiple. The Monte Carlo result reinforces the point: across {mc_n} Latin-Hypercube trials varying capacity factor, capex and opex, {mc_reach} reached the discount rate, the project IRR P90 was only {mc_p90}, and the equity IRR was undefined in {eq_undefined} trials and negative in {eq_p_neg} of the rest. The conclusion is robust precisely because it survives the optimistic end of every distribution tested.

The land-availability reality must close this discussion, because it reframes everything above. Even if a tariff, a financing package and a procurement strategy could be assembled to make the numbers work — and the breakeven analysis shows they cannot, not at this scale — there is no 10 MW of contiguous land at this urban, wetland-fringed parliamentary site to build upon. The most powerful lever, relocation to a dry-zone site, is therefore not optional refinement but the foundation of any viable project: it simultaneously secures the +15-20% yield uplift, opens access to the larger competitive tenders that carry the USc 8 USD PPA and capex economies, and provides developable land in the first place. The technology and procurement recommendation — Tier-1 bifacial n-TOPCon modules — remains sound and is not the problem; the problem is location, revenue and the cost of capital, in that order.

subheads.title: 11.1 Final Recommendation
paragraphs: Do not proceed with a standalone 10 MW solar PV plant at this site under current terms. This is not a marginal call requiring further refinement of the assumptions; it is a robust verdict that holds across every analytical lens applied in this report. The deterministic base case returns a project IRR of {fit_irr} under the likely SLSEA feed-in tariff of LKR {fit_lkr}/kWh and {comp_irr} under the best-achievable competitive USD PPA at USc {comp_usc}/kWh — both far below the {disc} discount rate. Project NPV is strongly negative in both regimes, at {fit_npv} and {comp_npv} respectively. The minimum DSCR of {fit_dscr} under the FiT, and {comp_dscr} under the competitive tariff at {gearing} gearing, confirms that the asset cannot, on its own cash flows, cover more than {comp_dscr_pct} of standard project-finance debt service. The investment case fails comprehensively, and it fails the same way under stress, under simulation and under structural optimisation.

It must also be stated plainly that the question is in one sense moot: there is no land here. The coordinates reverse-geocode to Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte — the Parliament Approach / Battaramulla area in Colombo District, beside the Diyawanna Oya wetland and the national Parliament. This is a dense urban and protected-wetland setting in which 10 MW of contiguous, developable land realistically does not exist. The site also sits in Sri Lanka's south-west wet zone, the cloudiest, rainiest and among the lowest-irradiance regions of the island. So even before the financial verdict, the physical and planning premises of a utility-scale plant at this exact location do not hold. The economic analysis that follows should therefore be read as a transferable template — a rigorous answer to the general 10 MW solar question — rather than as advice on a buildable proposal at these coordinates.

The four independent lenses converge on the same conclusion. The Monte Carlo simulation of {mc_n} Latin-Hypercube trials produces a project-IRR distribution of P10 {mc_p10}, P50 {mc_p50} and P90 {mc_p90}; {mc_reach} trials reach the {disc} discount rate, {mc_p_neg} return a negative project IRR, and the equity IRR is undefined in {eq_undefined} trials and negative in {eq_p_neg} of the rest. The one-way sensitivity tornado confirms the resource (capacity factor) and the tariff as the two dominant drivers, each worth {t_cf_pp} percentage points of project IRR for a ±10% change, with capex next at {t_capex_pp} points and opex and tax second-order. The gearing optimisation finds no gearing between {opt_lo} and {opt_hi} that meets the 1.30x DSCR covenant; equity IRR falls as leverage rises ({opt_eq_lo} to {opt_eq_hi}) — the signature of negative carry — while equity NPV rises by {opt_npv_gain} only because cheaper debt replaces equity and the sponsor funds up to {opt_cure_hi} of debt service the asset cannot cover; it stays deeply negative. No single pessimistic input is doing the work; the result is structural.

subheads.title: 11.2 The Binding Constraint Is the Asset, Not the Financing
paragraphs: The single most important analytical finding is that the limiting factor is the unlevered asset return, not the debt structure. The dedicated DSCR investigation makes this unambiguous. Sweeping the minimum-DSCR target from {dscr_lo}x to {dscr_hi}x under genuine debt-sculpting leaves the unlevered project IRR invariant at {dscr_proj_irr}, with NPV unchanged throughout. The DSCR is a financing-structure parameter that reapportions cash between lenders and equity; it is not a constraint on what the asset itself earns. At the ends of the band, a target of {dscr_lo}x admits more debt, lifting gearing to {dscr_gear_lo} with an equity IRR of {dscr_eq_lo}, while {dscr_hi}x reduces gearing to {dscr_gear_hi} with an equity IRR of {dscr_eq_hi}. Equity NPV, the measure the platform ranks on, is best at {dscr_best}x ({dscr_best_eqnpv}), but only {dscr_best_margin} better than at {dscr_cov}x, and neither measure is monotonic: both step at the {dscr_cov}x lock-up threshold. On both measures the equity is deeply negative at every target.

This has a direct implication for the 1.30x covenant. The 1.30x minimum DSCR is not the binding constraint, and it is not the problem. Relaxing it to admit more leverage would add little debt and would move the equity NPV by no more than {dscr_npv_span} across the whole band tested, in no consistent direction; just below the covenant, equity NPV is lower than at it, because distributions are then locked up until the debt is repaid. The corollary is that no amount of clever capital structuring rescues this project: the asset return of {comp_irr} sits {gap_pp} percentage points below the {disc} discount rate, and financing engineering merely redistributes a shortfall it cannot eliminate. That debt tenor has zero effect on the unlevered project IRR — a correct internal validation of the model — reinforces the same point from a different angle.

The breakeven analysis quantifies just how wide the gap is. The plant requires a tariff of roughly LKR {be_dscr_lkr}/kWh (about USc {be_dscr_usc}) merely to meet the 1.30x DSCR covenant, and roughly LKR {be_irr_lkr}/kWh (about USc {be_irr_usc}) for the project IRR to reach the {disc} discount rate. Those thresholds are about {be_dscr_x_fit} and {be_irr_x_fit} times the prevailing LKR {fit_lkr}/kWh FiT, and about {be_dscr_x_comp} and {be_irr_x_comp} times the competitive USc {comp_usc} benchmark. No tariff available to a standalone 10 MW project in Sri Lanka comes close to either figure. The economics are not finely balanced against a recoverable margin; they are structurally short by a multiple, driven by a modest resource (monofacial capacity factor 0.171, bifacial 0.182-0.183) in a low-irradiance wet-zone location combined with tariffs set well below the level this cost base requires.

subheads.title: 11.3 Recommended Sequence and Closing
paragraphs: If the sponsor wishes to pursue solar in Sri Lanka, the levers that can change the verdict should be pulled in order of power. First and most important, relocate to a dry-zone site in the north-east or south-east of the island — Vavuniya, Pooneryn or Hambantota — where the resource is materially stronger and yield improves by an estimated 15 to 20%. This single move addresses the dominant sensitivity driver, the capacity factor, and is the largest available lever; it also resolves the land and wetland-protection problems that make the present coordinates unbuildable. Second, secure a competitive USD PPA at scale, on the order of the USc 8.00/kWh Siyambalanduwa benchmark, which simultaneously lifts the tariff — the second dominant driver — and unlocks the capex economies that come with a larger, competitively tendered project.

Third, blend the capital stack and tender the EPC. Introducing DFI and concessional capital alongside commercial tranches lowers the blended cost of capital against which the asset return is measured, while a competitive EPC tender drives capex from the verified Sri Lankan utility-PV range of USD 1,100-1,350/kW toward the global frontier of roughly USD 700-900/kW — the third-ranked sensitivity lever. These three moves are complementary and, pursued together at scale and at a better site, are the credible path to a bankable solar investment in Sri Lanka. They are not, however, available to a sub-scale standalone plant at this location, which is precisely why the recommendation here is to redirect rather than to refine.

On technology and procurement, the recommendation is to retain the specified Tier-1 bifacial n-TOPCon module class. The primary selection — the Trina Vertex N TSM-NEG21C.20 at 720W, the only candidate datasheet-certified for both IEC 61701 salt-mist and IEC 62716 ammonia resistance, which is decisive for a coastal or wetland setting — is sound, as are the qualified alternates from Risen, Huasun and Astronergy. The engineering and equipment choices are appropriate and are emphatically not the source of the problem; the problem is the resource, the tariff and the location, in that order. In short: the engineering is sound but the investment case is not. The economics fail at this site under current terms, robustly and by a wide margin. The enduring value of the work delivered here is that the same model can be re-run in minutes against any alternative site, tariff or capital structure, so the sponsor can test the recommended dry-zone, competitive-PPA, blended-finance pathway quantitatively before committing a single dollar of development capital.
